blocks.x: I believe it's rolling now.
Let's get your name down until we know.
Is this for me, this mic here?
Yeah, that's for you.
I see. I'll keep my eye on the egg.
Let me move it closer back towards me. I see. You don't mind if I insult you?
If I talk strictly New Orleans, will that give a little highlight? Anything you want to do.
Yeah, just lean back and relax.
I think I'll be natural, Bergen.
Yeah, okay. Your name is what?
I was christened Stuart, S-T-U-A-R-T, Baker, B-E-R-G-E-N, Bergen.
Yeah. And you're now a senior, huh? Yes, sir. Yeah.
I came from Rome, this big Roman.
Well this is the second row of money. We were talking about money, how much money you made.
Oh come on, I've never made money in my life. I got all the gifts except the gift of making money.
But I mean, this is depression.

Oh yeah, we were playing at the Dharma Dance. It wasn't a prevelle, it was open air. I lived the second Spanish Forge, which location is now the Old Beach. Sometime we would make 35 cents a night. A fella named Ingehorn used to play with us out there. He was just starting with his metal clarinet. Charlie Storr, I met him out there. That's where I met Charlie, he'd sit in with us. Charlie Storr? Yeah, Starrer Storr.
Okay, Bergen we've got the third reel on.

In fact, Val was so used to using good musicians that one time I sat in with him and he heard a bad note and he kind of got on to me. So you can see the guy can always give you a good band. And it amazed me. I thought he didn't hear that note because I tried to bring it in with a chord to make it blend. Anyway I played with Barbera quite a while. And then after that, around 1937, some of the clubs we played in, Dick, was the old little club that used to be on Brown Street. And of course they rented it off of dancers. That thing was heavily draped all the way around with velvet and boy, the bigger the band the better it sounded. There was another place where the acoustics were very good, never did it sound too loud. And I'm trying to think after I left Frank, Barbera would have my daddy died if I let down. In the 40s? Yeah. I started drifting in little joints up on the airline highway, or Jefferson Highway. I think it was Vernon Roccaford had a job at a place called Joe's Inn, who was right across from the first O'Shaughnessy filling station, got a corner at the Tunkin Steakhouse. Joe Piccararo, he ran it. And I believe he ended up marrying Abby Brunas' first wife if I ain't mistaken. I believe his wife was Abby's wife at one time. And we had a good little band in there. We played a lot of the jazz tunes, and of course popular tunes too. And Joe Hellick played pretty good sax. We had Morris Escario piano. Big Bill Craig used to play. Not Bill Craigs but Bill Craig. And I had a bass player from out of town, but we had a pretty good band. I enjoyed playing there. And of course that band would break up and I'd go back there with another band. One time it was Steve Massico, Jeff Riddick, and Speck Reagan I believe, and myself. And that was about 1939. I can remember it very distinctly. And after 1939 I was – what happened about that time? Joe was in. Let's see.
39, yeah.

That's about the time I left Joe's Inn and the war came on. Yeah. We had the little business and before you know it all of the personnel that actually ran the business was in A1 classification with the draft board. I was the last one so I got a little deformity until I got somebody broken in to run the business. There's another case like music. I had a machine shop. I had a business. Just like music. But they were setting other guys up building machine shops for them and putting them in business so they could stay and make money. And I went. So I didn't take a bite. I'm still patriotic despite the way things are going. I guess I'd go again if I could. And during the war I couldn't get in any Coast Guard. I was in the Coast Guard. They had a nice band over, a big old band though. Something like the Blue Room Band over at St. Augustine. I saw old Roy Zinnerman over there, St. Augustine. He was playing with that band, with the Coast Guard Band. I was transferred to Galveston and they had an unrated band there but they got out of all the hard work and it was hard to get in too because I'd go around there and sit in and think that maybe I might get in the band and they'd be doing Guard Duty, you know?
It pays to play music.

It helps out a little bit. So I came back from the Coast Guard and I hadn't played for about a year or two and Leonard Wiley calls me and asks me if I wanted to play with the Leon Rapolo. Now not the original Leon Rapolo. This is the Leon Rapolo that used to direct the five piece band with the baton in the beginning. Don't laugh now. This is me recording. Okay I won't laugh anymore. You're laughing at my antics, not the- No, I just heard that story so many times. So anyway, it was good that I worked with him. I met Raymond Burke. I had never known Raymond until that time. You see the band we had, he booked a job across the river to Gay Parade. He had Rene Shea on piano, Eddie Chance on drum, Tom Brown on trombone, a bass fiddle I played, maybe trombone, maybe trombone, I don't know. I say trombone, myself and Raymond Burke. It was that five men and Leon. And then we worked up a pretty good little band over there. It wasn't bad at all. But things fell off. That's the way I started to go into business. I knew all the jazz men about that time and somebody asked me if I could get them a band. I said yeah. So I started using the fellas that I had met. And I think one of the first jobs I booked was myself and Raymond, a guy named Lou Castillo on drums, and Tester Craig played the bass fiddle, Gene Hemart played the guitar. And then I started using the name of Red Heart and his Red Heart band. I was about 48, 47, sometime around that time. And I worked up a pretty good band. I played at places called the Keyhole Across the River and I played at the Gay Parade with my own band. I played at a place called the Fun Bar, Jack Store. I used to come on television and advertise regular beer and do a few pantomimes. And then after that I went over to a place called the Wigwam for about a year. I'm talking about weekend jobs now in the last 15 years, all weekend jobs. We stayed at the Wigwam almost the whole year. Boy, I worked up a good band there. It was really the same band that I had at the Jack Store's Fun Bar. I had a good front line. I had a good front line. And that's one of my best tapes. That was made in 1951. And I have a tape. The fact that you've heard it, the Fun Bar tape, it was pretty good. The rhythm could have been a little stronger, but I had a good front line. And that's one of my best tapes. That was made in 1951. And anyway, after the Wigwam, which was a pretty nice place, I figured, well what are you going to do? I went to the dives again, so I said why don't you go in the union, I said that to myself, you might play in, you keep going up the ladder a little bit you know, because I'll play in all the voice places. Some places you'll have to light a match to see who's sitting next to you. But I went in the union and about the second day I was in I played a campaign job for Sheriff Tucker. He wasn't sheriff but he was running against Clancy. And that paid real good money. I was tickled to death. I was beginning to make money then. And I used the boys I'd play with, Raymond Bug, Tom Brown, Arnold Lugganer, and Eddie Chance and myself. We didn't use the piano. And that job brought me about three or four other campaign jobs for him, sort of a ballyhoo. And then I started to book some dance work, mostly in the union it's mostly spot dance, like conventions and fraternities. I played at St. Regis. Yeah I was in the union when I played at St. Regis for a while. And it was on it's way out then. There's another place I'm closing with my good music. But I wasn't the last man to play in there. And St. Regis. I kept on spotting as this itinerary says here. I don't know what's coming next but it's just about like it is right now. Spot jobs. I played New Orleans Country Club a few times. I played one jazz club dance. It seemed to be a little different though Dick. I still got the advertising and the paper. God bless the jazz club. They did a lot for jazz now. That's all I can say. But when I used to go to the jazz club Christmas dances, bring a 50 cent present and your dues card. But the night I played, oh boy. The atmosphere was the New Orleans Athletic Club. Goody goody. And it was five dollars a couple. And naturally it had a lot of empty tables. And everybody tried to make it, the way it looked to me, I'll take that, but not everybody. But there was no write ups about the dance and the magazine the next month. And I still say if they wouldn't have put that five dollars minimum on me, if you come and bring your card and your 50 cent present. And they had like old drawers like they used to have in the... Yeah. I'd have packed it too, because I had a good band that night. And to make it worse, before we started one of the officials came up and said give us some Christmas music. I'm there grooved up and geared up to play a jazz program, and this guy give us some Christmas music.
What's wrong though?
Pour a cold water, everything. I wouldn't say it was spiteful. I wouldn't say anything like that.
Well, we left out Tony Giardina, who was back before the band.

Oh boy, Tony Giardina. You're going back to 19 when your brother... You know when I quit that band? My old brother, I was trying to teach him trumpet when he was only about 14. He went to sleep on the bandstand. So Tony Giardina says, you're going to get that kid off the bandstand. I said, the kid don't, of course I was drinking them days. I said, the kid don't sleep there, I don't play. That was the end of my job. And my brother-in-law says, you were tough in them days. He's tough now. He's a big rascal. But he said, you were tough in them days. I don't know, I was a kid how you quit that job. But Tony had a pretty good band. He had Sajir Rod, he had Spike Legnan on bass, Charlie, what's Charlie's name? A drum player. I can't think of it. It wasn't Charlie Faber. Tony Giardina's wife played the piano. He had a pretty good library and he could really blow that clarinet on Panama. I remember the night I quit he said he was going to hit me in the head with the saxophone. I said, well don't hit me in the head with the clarinet because you sound pretty good on that. But he tolerated me. He was a nice guy and I was friends with him as long as he lived. But that was just a bad night for me, I guess.
Well, I liked his playing, huh?
He played good. He went up to Chicago with all those guys in the old days. I can't care if he had a drum player's name. Charlie what? He joined the Coast Guard Auxiliary during the war.
That was before I was here. Yeah.

So anyway I played, that was the old St. Bernard Country Club, three times a week I think it was, or twice a week. And I liked it. It was a pretty good job. I liked it. And I liked playing with Tony's band. Until he said my brother-in-law couldn't sleep. My mother-in-law is dead. But it was a good take. And I was always there.
Well, I jumped you back. But let's get back to about 1949 or 50.
50 or one of the Union I told you to have a place to talk. Yeah.
When I first heard you, almost one of the very first times anyway, which was some kind of deal up at Audubon Park and you had Harry and Tom Brown.

Well, I had a good band, yeah. None of us went in the Union at that time. That band later on went in the Union because they made some good tapes. Period. But the thing was I was playing, it was a parade first and it was a benefit baseball game, Burlesque, and we were running a jazz program in with it. And Doc Souchon was there. And I thought it was a good time to give Tom Brown a little recognition. So we gave him a little trophy and we figured, I wanted to put, Tom introduced jazz, you know, but we figured Pioneer of Jazz, which really isn't sufficient. It isn't. No.
So anyway we had an inscribed Pioneer of Jazz in Chicago or something.

Doc Souchon made the presentation. Bill Eastwood was playing banjo at that time. He played with a lot of the old time jazz guys too. But that's about the whole thing in a nutshell as far as that parade and the baseball game and the jazz presentation. But after that I lost those men. They were good musicians, they had a good band, but you can't keep a good man down. When I lose a man I say good luck to you, may you make money, and I start breaking into somebody else if I can't.

Yeah, well I remember then hearing you when you first were using Donald Sewer. Yeah. I guess right after that, sometime along in there. At some place, where was it? Was it back on Hagen Avenue? That's a lot of back. It was a little bit of speakeasy.

And I'll never forget you boys were recording my band and we had the recorder set up in the middle of the floor and some girl that Dutch knew, she got mad. She raised the devil because we were right in the middle of the floor without recording apparatus, but they didn't have anybody in there hardly. I don't see why we were offending them. Maybe they figured somebody might come in and want to dance and think they were not operating. But that piano was so badly out of tune Dick, it wasn't too good. And I think they had an exhaust fan in there. If you still have that tape or a record from it, you could almost hear a little fast vibration and Donald Sewer's notes on it. But that was back in 1950.
Bob Greenwood I think had the tape machine.

Oh Bobby, yeah. Bobby was there because we had a playback on it. But I think I gave all those records away I believe. The tape, I finally erased the tape and I still have part of it backwards. You know how you splice the tape backwards? As I told you, that's where I think that the patents for the original Bob came from. So they ran the tape backwards and they got the licks off, I'd say, and they used that timing. I really do believe it. Now Dick, I think we were up to 50, 1955, we were still in the union, playing spot jobs. Of course I met a lot of fire musicians, played with all the old timers. And up until about 65 everything was going good. And then I had a lot of teeth pulled. I might as well tell the public this because some of them know it. But I didn't realize my trouble was messing teeth back here. I started thinking that I had a bad mouthpiece, which was very stupid of me, after playing on a mouthpiece a few years. And I started changing mouthpieces. I went from bed. In two weeks I couldn't hardly play. I couldn't get a sound at the heart. And it took me about three years to realize that I had to tighten up twice as hard on the right side of my mouth because there's nothing, no vibration, no foundation for these muscles to rest on. You lost your back molar.
Yeah, two of them in the back.

And I always had two missing hip. When I lost these two that did it. So I think I can play about 90% of how I used to play, but I can't get up there and get those high notes anymore. But maybe if I played every night in a week I could probably do it, but that'll never happen again. In fact that hasn't happened in the last twenty years or maybe thirty years. But when you play every night you do get much better on a horn. Now any recording you've heard of me, especially since I've been in the union, right now these recordings you hear some of those tunes we haven't played in six months, no rehearsal. Some of them, not all of them. But I'm not booking much work. I don't think I've ever booked over twenty-six jobs a year since I've been in the union. That's the average happening in the week. Most of us twenty-six come into winter time and summertime sometimes you go a month or two without work. Of course I have to work in the daytime. I can't get on the phone all day like some of these guys can do. You know, look up jobs and nobody ever throws me a lead. That's how I'm not that lucky. But I've always enjoyed playing and I don't guess I'll ever quit. I'm about to bring this thing to a close, Alan.
You're playing in the church sometimes. Oh, I've got plenty more. I've got a band.

I have one tape I made with some of the fellas from the church. But I still got it. It sounds pretty good. A fellow named Kurz, Alan Kurz, played the mellophone. And Orwin Kurz used to play at Club Forest with Jules Baduk. Orwin Kurz. And he and I and his son got it. It sounded like the Salvation Army band. But it was pretty good. But as far as playing in churches, kid, I don't play in churches.
I was going to ask you, speaking of no rehearsals, remember when you played the Queen Anne room at the Montaléon?

Pick? I appreciated that job. It was one of the nicest jobs I ever played in my life. Orwin called me and said, hey Stuart, I've got a job, will you come in with me? He says, you have the tax numbers for reporting the tax and everything. I said, delighted. He says, I have a drummer. I said, well, okay. He says, can you get the men? I said, I can get the men that played last Saturday with Shark. I said, I've been giving them more work than Shark had. That time I was. He says, no, we can't use the two Christians. It was Emil on trombone and Earl on clarinet. He says, we can't go back with those two guys, too. I said, well, Shuck saw him. I said, I'll have to get fellas I played with a couple of years ago. And it was my name, I'd say it's the best deal I ever had on advertising. Orman Hugg, one of the greatest piano players I could have played with. And I have to go there with a band I haven't played with. Well I've never played a job with Orman up to that time. And I didn't even know the drummer. And I get Hooper out of retirement. And I only had about one night. I said, Hooper, let's run over a couple of tunes at least we're going to open up with. Charlie Hartman, I got him out the country. He had just left me. And I did have a little chink on bass that night. So we go down there and you know Dick, I know the value or I know how to appraise playing. But after that was over, he had some guy there that loved the way I played. And nobody was drinking so Hugg came up and said, great Stu. Boy this is one interview I'm glad I have. Hugg said, great Stu. I said, what do you mean Orman? He says, there's one guy here that thinks you're greater than Hurt. And I said, man how ridiculous can he be? So I happened to meet that man when it was all over. And he said, oh I sure enjoyed it. He said something about my playing was symmetrical. And he had a few drinks. He was with his lady friend. And I told him, I said, how ridiculous can you be? And the guy actually got married with me because I didn't agree with him. But that was the nicest compliment. But gee whiz, I can't even carry Hurt's horn. The kind of stuff he plays. But apparently this fella liked what I played. And that job paid good and it was over at 12 o'clock I believe. And I told Chink, I said, boy I could take one of these every Sunday. That was the end of it. And uh...
Yeah I think Pinky had something to do with it.
Pinky was the MC. And of course you had Jeff and somebody else on the side when we were taking intermission. Yeah I remember. But it was a nice job.

You know I had a guy all the way from Australia with me that night. He was an impressive man. Nick Politis. He's a New Orleans style clarinet player from Australia. And his parents are from Greek. He's got a combination.

Well if I would have had Mr. Christian and Earl, you would have heard stuff that would knock off sound. It would sound like we're reading it almost. Of course we can put more feeling to music when you play by ear. You can't hardly read jazz music. In fact these tunes I play if I tried to read them I probably couldn't.
Yeah. You have down here about the steam of President.

Well I had played on the steam of President and I was going real good until I told the Captain I quit. So the night I quit I took another trumpet player on because just nothing wasn't coming out the horn. And Willie Gerbrecht said he'd give me a hand so I'd play a number and he'd play a number. But I let Willie play as much as he wanted to. And it was about five years before I contacted him. I've been playing off and on when the other band takes off. I played for the Captain about six times last year and a couple of times this year so far. But he likes the band. He would have got me back if I'd have been playing since I came back. But I don't try no real high notes anymore. I try to keep it like Bobby Hackett you know? And he's one of the world's best. And I don't try to go too high, overplay the horn. I think the public likes it a little bit better, Dick. The public doesn't always appreciate these gymnastics we do on a trumpet.
They don't.

And I've been able to put the band across. I've been having a good man in my band. I might tell you my last lineup that I had when we played since Monk Hazel died I went with Emil Oyssen on drums. This is my latest band. I've been using Bobby Coquille on bass fiddle and I still have Bill Voorhees on piano. And my front line is Earl Christian, Emil Christian and myself. And they know my routine, they know my endings, the breaks. In fact Earl comes over here about every once a month and we just play together. Sometimes like Bill Voorhees wanted to come last night but Earl Christian had his horn out of Joe Grasavis getting fixed. But we like to present a real good jazz program and we're proud of the fact that we're from New Orleans. If anybody hears it, we wanted to hear it played the way we played it in the old days. And we're always trying to play it good. We never did try to think that we were too good at calling up a tune and calling it jazz. There are too many of the reading bands that do that. I'm talking to good reading bands. As soon as they go into a jazz tune, they call it up as if they're too good to play it right. And they play it willy as we used to say in the old days. But jazz music has to have a feeling to each note, a feeling to each beat, and it's got to be right. Well Dick, I enjoyed this conversation and you know I'm a man of few words.
You know we left a lot of stuff out. We haven't really got started yet. Do you have enough energy to go on?
Yeah, after a couple of coffee, because I'm just getting started Dick.
Yeah, we left out WDSU TV.
Oh yeah. I got to tape on out if you ever want to hear that.
Good.
That's another night I got a bad break.
Can you turn it off for me?
Yeah, he can turn it off. We'll get some more coffee. Sure.
All right, we were talking about WDSU. You.

Well, there was a man in the advertising business, Dick. His name was John...I can't think of his last name. John what? John Curran. No, uh-huh. Anyway, he was Shep Morrison's brother-in-law. Big old fella. Nice guy. And he gave me a ring about one o'clock in the day and said he needed a band or a try-off at WDSU. Parade of Bands. That was the name of the program was the Parade of Bands sponsored by Barnett Furniture Company. So, I told him I sure would. I'd like to play it. I get on the phone. I can't get in touch with Tom Brown. I can't get in touch with a couple other guys. So, I introduced myself over the phone to Digger Lane. I said, Digger, you don't know me but I know you and I got a good deal coming up and we make the grade. I said, can you be at WDSU about three feet? And I lined the band up. Jake Chambry on piano. Sherwood wasn't doing anything. I got Sherwood, Charlie Fabright and Ram and Booth. While we go down there and naturally I called tunes that we all knew and it seemed to go over pretty good, Dick. And I told Johnny, I keep saying Johnny Conley, it wasn't Conley though, his name wasn't Conley. And he was timing the tunes as we played them and before you knew it we had the schedule all made up. He said, the job is yours. And we go the next night to play. And of course, it never did happen before in his life but while he was playing Sherwood Man Japan's the bridge and his bass fiddle breaks. And then he thought, during the commercial, he thought the camera was pointing one way and he walked right behind him with his bass fiddle doing a commercial. It looked good though, that was a good kick. We didn't know it and he didn't know it so I guess he did the right thing. He had to get the bass fiddle fixed. And with the extreme air conditioning there, right in the middle of a chorus my mouth went so dry I could hardly play. And just lucky I got through that chorus and I had to have a glass of water concealed in the room so I could take a sip of it every once in a while when the camera was off of me. And there was only one bad thing about that. It could have maybe helped me to climb the ladder a little bit but whoever was in charge of that program at that time, they were more interested in concealing the microphone to make the picture look good than in the quality of music they were putting out. So you know yourself when you see me play I usually hold the horn up about on a fifteen degree angle towards the ceiling. Well they put a microphone right by my belt buckle. And I was blowing loud that night. I mean I was blowing so loud that one guy said, can you cut it down a little bit, they're rehearsing in the next studio. Now this is when we were broadcasting. So I was just tickled to death that I sounded so strong you know. And when Raymond plays he usually bends down and Raymond was playing harmony to me right in the microphone. And I was blowing up to the ceiling over the mic. And Diggalane he played down on the other side right in the microphone. Well when I got home and one of my friends said, what's the matter with you? You're weak. We could hardly hear you. Oh man that broke my heart almost. Because I was blowing. If he had a boom, a boom mic about five or ten foot away from me I would have blasted the place out. And one of my friends taped that program for me and when I got home and I heard it, I still have it. Unless I'm playing by myself, even when I play by myself the tone is dead. You know, coming off the back wall. The wall was about thirty feet away from us, the back wall. And it was one of the biggest disappointments of my life, in spite of the fact that I don't think I made any clinkers at all, and I was very nervous. And the band wasn't too bad. Raymond played good, Diggal played good. I played my heart out. The rhythm section was all right. But the trumpet had a dull, dead tone to it when you could hear it. The reception was real bad. And those boys, if I had anything against them, which I know it was just tough luck, but they got even with me if they had anything against me. But I know they did. It was just a case of the technicians wearing on the ball. But everything went all right and we got through it. Oh, incidentally, guess who my guest artist was on that program? Blind Gilbert. Oh, really? Yeah, I have him on that tape. He sang After You're Gone, as one of our friends would say, After You're Gone. You know what I mean?
I remember that.

It sounded like a street in a French quarter. Not do, man. He was gone. And he takes a break, one of those goofus breaks, and he plays his guitar. We're still talking about Blind Gilbert. And he did all right. We made a little extra life to the program. So that was back in 1951 or 1952, Dick, I guess. About 52.
You got 53 down on this piece of paper.
A half an hour show there. Yeah.
This is real. I just got a minute on it.
So why don't I run this off and put on a new one before we get into anything else? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Okay, it's going on the fourth reel now, Barry.

Dick, around 1954 I remember. Basin Street Six had really split up. I think Gerard formed his own band, but Pete and Joe Rodas, Bonnie Franks, they kept that name, Basin Street Six. And they were playing I think where Soul City is today, on Jefferson Highway, Airline Highway. And their regular band was Connie Jones was playing trumpet instead of George, and they had Johnny Edwards on drums instead of Charlie Duke. Outside of that the band was the same. But this kid Connie Jones had to go to National Guard, and Pete Fountain had to go to National Guard. So they asked me if I'd play two weeks with them, and I was on a one week vacation. So I told them I'd play as long as I could, but I was really getting ready to the Reeve Town on a Wednesday. So I started on a Saturday night, I played. I played the matinee Sunday, and I played Sunday night, Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday. I kind of told them Tuesday that I thought I'd have to, that I could get them another trumpet player. I think Nick Beninati went after me. But the first night there, Connie Jones was not there the first night, but Pete Fountain was. That was the only time I ever played with Pete. And Pete played the first night, that Saturday night. And it was me and Pete and Joe Rodas in the front line, Johnny Edwards, Bonnie Franks, and Zinneman on the piano. The next evening I went there, Pete had left and they had Fano Rapallo. You ever hear Fano Rapallo? Oh yeah. You know what I mean? I haven't one tape. I taped that. It didn't come out too good. And we played most of the tunes that they played. But I noticed they played some of the tunes in different keys. It's funny how a group gets together. And standard tunes too. Sometimes I'm accused of playing some of the, one or two tunes I like a different key better than the original key that they played in, or the old timers played in it. But that's the way it goes. Anyway it was pretty good. I enjoyed it very much. Unfortunately though I had to leave after about three nights. But Nick Beninati played and finished the week out and they seemed to be satisfied.
While we're talking about different things we didn't get into Lester Nelson very much. He's a guy that I hear people talk about and don't know much about him.

Now we're going back to about 1933 or 34. At the Rialto Club is where I met Lester Nelson. Real good looking guy Dick. On order of Charleston Heston you might say on that order. Maybe not as big. Real fine looking man. He had a wonderful ear for harmony. He didn't read. He was a guy. And I don't remember his, I don't know how he's driving like Murray used to drive on tenor. We call him riding the beat. Yeah. But I know one thing everybody said that he was one of the best team up men going on tenor. And we heard one night at the Woodman Hall we weren't playing. And another guy we heard Harry Shields, Steve Massico and this Lester Nelson. Three sax team sounded like they were reading. Beautiful harmony. Those fellas were all naturals. But Lester Nelson he finally ended up making flyers for fish hooks. He was very famous for that. And then later on he got sick and died. He always had stomach trouble even when I played with him back in 1933 or 34. He had stomach trouble. But he was a good looking guy and he played fine. But he was strictly for a small man.
Who did he sound like as we know through records? Anybody in particular?
I'll tell you maybe my ear wasn't developed then but I never could put him in a category. I don't know why.
Maybe he's original. I don't know.
I don't know. You'd have to ask Harry Shields maybe. Harry played with him plenty.
And what about Solistan's trumpet player?

You were talking about the little guy. Who was that? I don't know who he was. I really don't know. But I know when he shook it and blew. That was over in Pensacola, Florida when they passed through for one night. And boy the little guy leading their band. If the band would make a scream at the end of the court he'd jump up in the air and come down. I mean he could put a band across himself even without a band behind. He was terrific. That's the way they led bands in those days. Well Cab Calloway used to jump on.
Would he be there with a baton or something?
I don't know. Maybe he had a baton but man he was lively. All kind of gymnastics he might say he went through.
In other words they hit it and then he jumped way up in the air and get out of the floor. I'm going to hack this thing out.
If I don't I can't retaliate it the right way.
About twenty years ago I remember we were talking about your cook. Didn't your cook have a friend? That was Melinda.

That's when I had to see and know about Cornette. You can go again twenty years ago. That's when I was around twenty. Well you told anybody. Yeah. But Melinda used to cook for us and she knew a young man by the name of Ernest Johnson or Ducky Johnson or something like that. Ducky Ernest. Yeah. Ducky Ernest. And he played with the marching bands. The Buzzards was about three blocks from my house and we'd see them playing maybe Malifaux with the Buzzards, whatever band it was that played for the Buzzards, maybe the Eureka. I think it was the Tuxedas in those days.
The night of bands.

And when my sister was coming out we hired a band and he got the band for us. I was only a kid. I only had a bugle. Maybe I didn't even have a cornet then. Or maybe I did. I guess I might have had a cornet. I don't know. Did you? Go ahead. They had a pretty good band. It was a pretty good band. He played the bass field that night.
Did you tell me something about Guy Kelly once? Did you ever know him? No.
I don't remember a trumpet player. I know one thing, Dick, I don't know how corny it was but he used to have a band at Lane's Mill when I was a kid. You all probably never did hear of those guys.
No.

He had Eddie, you know Lefty Armand, who played in the bass field. He could tell you a lot about it. One of his brothers played in that band, whether it was Paulie or Louie, and you had a band, and Kling, old man Kling played the bass fiddle, and Clown Alphys played the cornet. And Lane's Mill in those days was going real fast, you know? And they had their own little, like these big companies have their own little recreation club, and they had like the dance hall, or the hall for entertainment upstairs and they had a swimming pool downstairs. But it might be of interest to you, because these guys were from uptown, and somebody like Lefty Armand still living to get a little information on that band. I doubt if you all have anything on it.
I doubt that we do too.
Lane Mill band. I think Eddie Cooney played the drum.
I haven't seen Allen in years. Cack, probably Cack Riley. Cack Riley has pictures in that book.

I used to play with Cack once in a while, go home and get the cornet, when this boy used to have Lion of Laurel, it used to be George Stokes, they'd put a nickel in his lot in the March of the Bobcats. Cack would get his trombone, walked around, I'd go and get the trombone, they'd have a few beers you know.
The place is monsters now you're talking about.
That's right. But I only live two blocks from there.
We still go there every time.

Well I have to go down to Mardi Gras if I want to see somebody I know. And most of the Mardi Gras parades, the marching parades meet there. And I used to play ball in that lot, and have my own team in one town.
And you played ball and cornet at the same time?

No. The league was open and George talked, and George says, get us a band. We got a band like Bill Craig and a couple of other guys. We opened the day, put the trumpet down, ran the pitcher's box without warming up and start pitching. But we lost that day. And guess the name of my team, Jake? What? The cheeky man. The cheeky man?
The cheeky man.

The cheeky guy is supposed to be a nervy guy, you know. Cheeky. Let me your automobile, I want to go up to Baton Rouge. That's after you were married in 1938. Yeah, that was after around 1938. Well they had a real fine ball player named Bull Raw. I used to pitch for the Pelicans. He was sitting at the meet and he said, you can't use that name. I said, what's going to stop me? A little cheeky man. I think we were sabotaged.
Who made the sweatshirts for you?
We bought them and we stenciled them.
Tell me about somebody like Boisau. Did you hear many piano players like that when you were coming up?

Boisau's style, when I was coming up I didn't go for it because everything was Father Hines when I was coming up. And if you didn't play like Father Hines, the closest thing to Father Hines was a fellow I played with by the name of Dizzy Norman. Later on he was with Bois Maesick. He was not with Bois Maesick, yeah, when I played with Bois Maesick. But Dizzy could play just like Father Hines. But the only thing, he didn't give you a good beat when you were playing. He kind of rambled around the back.
Butterfly?
I like a piano player that takes the pace. When I'm playing, just like the old banjo that gives you the beat, I like a piano player to turn into a rhythm and chord progression instrument.
No butterfly.

But Dizzy kind of butterfly in the band. You'd have to have extra good drum and a bass fiddle player to push the band. But a piano player can push a band. Because I know I play with piano, drums and trumpet. And all you've got is the piano and the drums and you play them. And so many piano players think that's too simple. They don't want to do it. And other ones can't do it. They don't know when the changes come in. So they have to stick to the melody so they don't get lost. But you find all kinds of music. All of them can be good musicians but they're just down on one thing.
Well I remember Boisot had a funny, what did you call it, a wandering bass or something?

Boisot, he had a good left hand. He had sort of a Dixieland bass because he'd go, you know, like that. He filled in his old time bass. I have some nice tapes. He stayed at his place one night and I have about almost an hour of his recordings with nobody around. They're fun. If you ever want to listen to them or copy one of them, be glad to let you copy them.
Oh I loved it.

Beautiful tunes too. They're not all jazz tunes. And some of them are like Red Rose Rag. I didn't even hear of it. But still they only played some beautiful tunes. In the old days you had a voice to a tune before you come to the chorus. And let me call you sweetheart. I didn't even know I had a beginning, a voice. And he plays the voice to each one of these waltzes. He used to come over here to practice. Oh he was one of my good friends. He practiced with me. He was a fine old gentleman. We had fun. Boisot was a good guy.
Good man.

Well you had a day job then near his place, huh? Yeah, I was 422 common and he was 424 driver. But I met him at the jazz club though. And one day I happened to see him in the neighborhood and I was amazed how I worked so close to him. And he was a fine old gentleman.
You've been at that same place, Kittredge Waters, for years now?
Yeah, I left Woodward and White. My daddy died in 1938. They needed someone. And I said well I better go where I belong.
Your daddy was there before you at Kittredge Waters?

Yeah, my dad went in with Kittredge Waters. He was one of the founders. He was that hyphen in the middle, you know, Kittredge-Waters. My daddy did pretty good. We lived in a poor neighborhood, but I was a little rich boy in a poor neighborhood. We had all the balls and the gloves and man, that house we lived in, I'd love to have it right here, on Sony Ant-Laurel. It's a three story house with marble fireplaces, about 12 foot ceilings, about 18 to 20 foot hall ceilings, mahogany stat rail. All the antiques my mother had, like the big mirrors and all, we really don't know what to do with them. My sister had to cut the top off of one of them.
Give them to me, I'll take it.

But I was almost like a little rich boy in a poor neighborhood. Because more of my friends were poor and I didn't want that title, you know, being a sister. So I had to out-case them, out-fight them, because I'd go out dressed like Lord Fauntleroy and I had to let them know I was tough before I went outside. And I got along with them, maybe that's why I was always for the underdog. They were all good boys, some of them went bad and some of them came out pretty good. But they were all my friends, no matter what they turned out to be. And when I was a kid I liked them. They were all right. They were good kids.
I know when we were looking at your scrapbook we were talking about different musicians and I don't want to mention any names, but some of them went to the top and some of them didn't, huh?

Yeah, they could be. You know Dick, let's just say, there's a word for it, self-control you might say, and over-indulgence. And it could be three or four things. Some of them like to go, some of them like to gamble, some of them like to drink, and some of them like to smoke. The wrong kind of cigarettes. And unfortunately somebody has to pay for it and some of my friends did. And you could almost see it coming.
What about Louis Armstrong? You say you like Louis, but there's a lot of Louis's really. I mean through the years there's many different kinds of Louis Armstrong.
I'm glad you clarified that because I was thinking about that when I said Louis. When I say Louis, that means Louis Armstrong. If I mean prim, I say prima.
Yeah.
But we always did say play like Louis plays. Every time I've mentioned it on this interview Louis, I met Louis Armstrong.
But I mean there's many different styles. I mean Louis, which style do you like?

Well Louis, to me, he had the best style. Now Eldridge, I thought he was terrific. I didn't hear Eldridge on too many records, but After You're Gone, Eldridge made a terrific record on After You're Gone. I even heard James on one or two records and it sounded pretty jazzy to me. He had a different style when he was with, what you call his band, Goodman's band. I didn't like that style too much, but it made him. But on a record I have with him and Coleman Hawkins I believe, he sounded pretty good.
But back to Armstrong, what tunes do you like that Louis made?
Well naturally I liked West End Blues. But I have a record Mr. Our Mr. Ambassador or something like that.
Ambassador Sands.

And Muscat rambles out of this world man. It's terrific. And I think I like that better than that. They have good teamwork too. The band hits it off good with him and he plays a lot of good. Of course he throws in a few little tunes but he dresses them up so nice that they're jazzy. They're not just inserting a couple of measures of another tune. He makes them fit in right. I used to always like Someday You'll Be Sorry. I thought it was very fine. And I have a lot of records that you're probably not up on like Red Rose, Red Nose, Red Cap, on a little beach in Wakalu, Hawaii or something like that. Anyway he plays terrific stuff on these records. You know I like those Hawaiian things.
A little bamboo bridge. To you sweetheart. He plays good stuff.

To you sweetheart. You know that brother-in-law that went to sleep when he was 14 years old on a bandstand? When he got to be about 25 he'd never be playing a band but he'd take his trumpet and he'd play all them Louis, you know the ones that weren't too high? You know those easy ones like on a little bit. And he had them down pretty good. But he'd have to learn something by heart real good because you'd jump meter. It's a funny thing. Some musicians jump meter. Oh boy that's something. You can't really correct that.
What about you called yourself Red Hot at one time and then the Society Six came out. How did that happen?

When I was a little kid I always did like Devil Ham. You know anything? Trademark is the Devil. And I said what can I do for a name that will be before the public in other subjects, other phases? Like a Red Hot sale going on. So I must have seen that one day. So I said Berg if you go ahead and take the name of Red Hot, every time somebody uses a Red Hot sale going on they'll be thinking of you and they'll tie it in. So I got Harold Dutter, drove me the Devil blowing the trumpet, dancing on the coals and all.
It went pretty good.

In fact, Dick, one of the reasons why I dropped that name after about four years, there was some band playing at the Druids. Now I don't want to get in trouble here. But the Druids was raided on the counter that was Indecent Dance and the something. And after it was raided it was in the paper. And then later on, I still have it, I find a hand bill that they throw around in your yard, music by a red hot band, Druids. And I know my kids were getting kind of old then. I said, well boy, that's one reason why you ought to get out of it. But I must have been pretty good at trying to make the public think I'm playing that music. And the next thing was, I'd go to try to book a pretty good formal wedding, whether the husband or the daddy would spend a lot of money on a trousseau and a couple of thousand dollars for this and that.
And a week and a half of your band, Red Hot and his Red Hot trumpet, it just didn't fit in.

So I said, well I'll tell you what I'll do. We'll go from the beer drinking department to the champagne department. I'll call the band the High Society Six. High Society tied in with the old jazz tune and then to be facetious about it, trying to get in with the silk stocking gang. So I thought I was killing two birds and one stone. And then I started playing hotels where I got to use eight men. So I've ditched the High Society Six. It's Stu Bergen and his New Orleans style music. And that's all I can do.
I was going to ask you about different tunes that you like in particular.

Well it all depends on how you feel, Dick. When your lip is right you like the ones you're going to show off and not make any clinkers. But there's a lot of good tunes, Dick. Now Chris and I, we practice a lot together and Chris likes Wolverine blues. And Chris likes Big Bud and Eggman the way we play it. And he knocks hell out of the Hindu stand. But that's a crip. That's as easy as the Saints. And I used to really like Deed I Do. It's a Tin Pan Alley tune, but I always did like it. Sleepy down the South I always liked. Of course the range is a little high for me now. I used to take it up to around the high C anyway. I'd stick between the G's and occasionally an F. I mean an A. But I don't go too high anymore. But that was that tune we were trying to record up at Tulane. It came out so scratchy and we'd give it to you good before you leave. But those are wonderful. Someday you'll be sorry. And of course the blues. Everybody loves the blues. And I like it slow in E flat and I like to pick it up in the key of F. Now that's one of my idiosyncrasies. It's not an idiosyncrasies, but it's something that's stupid but makes me feel better if I do it. Which is the definition of an idiosyncrasies.
What about She's Crying for Me? Why did you ever pick that tune up?

Well when I was learning how to dance when I was about sixteen or seventeen, Nick LaRocka used to play up into Octavia with a guy named Wynn. And when they left, Sal Majada and Sam Majada, the Triangle Band, came in. And I could see old Sal was the trumpet. Sam and, what is Sal and Sam?
Tony was the trumpet. Tony, Tony.

Cornette Tony. The Cornette player had a bent mouthpiece because he'd hold his horn down. And he'd hold his handkerchief because he'd sweat, he wasn't coughing off a little. And he'd put the horn out the window. The bandstand was here and the window was here for the first tune. And the guy hit the cymbal, bang! And we used to call him Monk. Abbey Brunis, the drum player, his brother Moon, a monk, whatever you want to call him. He'd come over to my place and we'd reminisce about the old Octavia and he'd say,
Yeah, the Machado on the corner and stick it out the window.
What did you do to the down there? Bang! How about that? He'd make you laugh.
This is Abbey the drum.
Abbey's drum brother. I said his brother.
Oh, his brother.
I never did know him. Oh, he was a kid. He was a pretty great comedian. He knew all the old jazz tunes. He'd make fun of Better Than That's There. Yeah. Uncle Abbey.
Yeah, I don't remember. Uncle Abbey. He was a pretty great comedian.
Well, they knew Santa. Yeah.
No point in putting that down. I don't know.
He was a kid.

I don't know his real name, but he was a kid. He'd always, usually brighten up my day when he'd come in, because as soon as he'd come in he'd hit on a desk. Let's have it. Da da da da da da da da da. That's the way he was.
Well, that was Henry was that guy, wasn't it? No, I remember.
It was Abbey Brunis, the drum player's brother. Yeah. I can't, we called him Monk. I remember him. We called him Monk. He had a big chin.
Yeah, I remember.
Joe Mraz calls him Moon. Yeah. We called him Monk.
Speaking of Monks, how many Monks were there around?

The only Monks I knew was Monk Hazel. I didn't meet him until later in life. And Monk Myers played saxophone I didn't know. And Norman Myers, some guys called him Monk Myers when he was in Jesuits. I don't know. Was Monk Hazel a ball player? Monk Barone was a ball player but he played saxophone a little bit in the old days. But Monk Hazel, he went to Jefferson School, I don't remember him there. Maybe he was a little older than me though.
Did he play any good? Who? Monk Hazel.
Man, you hear them tapes I got? Yeah. That's what made the tapes. Monk inspired you to play. You'd have to hold me on the bandstand sometimes. When you play with Monk you're jumping.
Monk makes you jump when you play.

He's everything they said about him. And I mean it proves it. I had one tape where I think he enjoyed playing with me because when we finished playing he said, wowee! And I know Monk, he told me at one time we had the best spot in jazz band in town. Coming from him I appreciate it. Because he was sitting in, not sitting in, but playing off nights in the quarter at that time. Yeah, Monk was a kick. But he sure could beat those drums.
Did he drink when he was with you?

I must say that his mother had just died and twice he drank a little bit. Both times he finished the jobs with me. And he might have had a little bit too near the end, but he finished the job, he got home, and I couldn't complain. And there's a funny thing, it was a year apart and it was the same job at the same place where it happened. In other words I booked the job one year and the next year I booked it and it was booked in the same place. And two times it happened. In fact on some of the jobs I had some big shots helping me out, you know, to play with my band. And he knows them real good. And he was saying, look at them, drinking. How are they going to play their horn?
How are they going to play their horn?

Yeah. He was almost a, what do you call it, who was that old lady? One of the Carrie Nation's boys there for a while. Yeah. When he was playing with me. Yeah, I had no trouble with Monk. Yeah. Showed up on every job and gee whiz anybody can drink twice in a year. Sure.
Oh, back to this business about copying and all that and saying different things. How do you develop your own ideas? Because I know some of your licks are original and all that.

That's a funny thing. I don't know Dick. It's spontaneous the first time. And if it records on your brain, you probably get it a second time. And it's hard to tell because you can't play anything. In other words, I'll play along Armstrong style, but like Big Bud and Eggman, I might touch on one or two of his licks. But don't forget I'm playing about three choruses and there's what, 32 measures to a chorus and I'm not hitting him note for note. And like you say, I got my own licks in there. I don't know. I try to play on the beat. I try to follow the chord progression. It's like touch typing. Patterns, or music is like that. That's why I don't use false fingers. Some trumpet players are exploits in false fingers. That would mess up my pattern because each tone is a certain key on the way I play. And if I start using false fingering, my tone isn't going to be that key, see? And my fingers make a certain pattern and that's a lick. And of course it coincides with the timing and the tone of the scale. But it's hard to say. It's the way or where it comes from. It comes from all of these cosmic forces. I don't know. I don't know what to say. It comes to you though. And some of them you like. Now I noticed on Butter and Eggman I hit a couple of licks on there that I haven't hit any one to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember
to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember

to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember I've got to give him all the credit I can give him, because if I had to choose the most authentic New Orleans style trumpet player right now, it would be Sharky. However, when I was coming up, maybe I had my sights set higher than that. First thing, I knew Sharky couldn't play Louis Range. I knew that. So as good as Sharky was, I'd like to play better than Sharky if I'd have made it. Maybe I never did touch Sharky as far as it goes. But anyway, you hear a lot of talking about Sharky. We liked his, now he had a chorus on High Society, you know, Bo-da-loo-da-dee, Bo-da-loo-da-da-da, Bo-da-loo-da-da-da. That made him really, that didn't happen to put him on the map. Because when I was in high school we used to try that once in a while. Of course we didn't play good enough to go through with it and I didn't have the record. Once in a while I'd try it, you know, and see how far I could go. But later on I started playing Piku's chorus on the trumpet, you know, Bo-da-loo-da-dee, Do-da-dee. Donald Seuss says, how can you do that? Well when I get to the middle I'd inject some of all the stuff around it. You know, instead of beat-bomb-bomb-bo-da-loo-da-doo-da-doo. But I played that chorus when I was young. But the only one that really ever stopped me was When You're Smiling One Octave Higher. I never did do a good job on that. That was a little too hard. And I didn't have a lot of notes, it was just a call for a good lip and a lot of energy and endurance.
You know, while I'm talking about all these tunes I forgot one. Who featured T.O. Sand?
Down here? Mike Trapani I believe was the guy that kept playing it. And of course it was old then. Now they might have played it out at Spanish Fort in the old days, I don't know.
Well I used to have Francis Murray play it.
Yeah, well he played with, I played that tune with him, he might have it on a record in the jazz club.
I don't think so.

I think Francis one time and Bill Kress played a job with Mike Trapani and he liked that tune and I believe that's where they started playing it. And if I'm not mistaken, Pete Font was at the club that night and wanted to know the name
of that tune.
That was a long time ago. I don't think Pete was still maybe with Al Hood at that time, with the bass of Street Six
maybe.

I don't know, maybe it was with Street Coins and the Font. But now you take George Gerrard, now you get a little inspiration from George. Everybody would say how he drove, how he drove on the beat. When I'd go on the job I'd say, well man if George is driving buggy you have to drive a
little harder.

But George, I thought he was terrific. His tone was almost too good for jazz. But he didn't like it. He wanted to get a tone like I got. He was trying to find a pea shooter trumpet and I said boy don't change. He was terrific. Of course he didn't have the range Armstrong had. And I'm very George, I thought he was the best we had. And I still think my idea that the bass of Street Six was the best New Orleans band we had in the last twenty years. Well I mean Sharky had a good know. Sharky's band, you know with the Caravan, was it Dudley LeBlanc's Caravan, Paticone, that was a good band. But the bass and Street Six they could do things in the Sharky's Band. They could play sweet tunes, the Pazola's tunes. Now I classify the comics secondary with the bass and Street Six. Because you know anybody around town trying to make up a band to sound equally as good as they sounded? You have a mighty hard time doing it. And I've read ratings where they rate them as a comedian band. It's an insult to every one of those boys. It was a fine band. And right today I get my band as close to the bass of Street Six as I can.
And I get the little Louie, throwing it on the Louie Tones. You got energy enough for one mower?
Yeah, buddy.
You got enough questions? I don't know if I have enough questions, huh?
That's alright, son.
But we can get a little bit of it in anyway. I didn't think we'd get this far, man.
What does Joe Morazz call me, honey? I made him mad one night up at the jazz club. You know I call you. Joe Morazz calls me, we the people. We the people.
Shut up, we the people.
Don't put ants on him.
We the people, you know.

He never stops. I'm not worried about that. I'll drop in and see him once in a while, Dick. If you don't play like his brother, you don't play it right. He tells the guys what he wants when he has it. Dick, when he has a record made. D dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear

I got the fifth reel going. Anyway, Fergie. So let's eat. How about it? Yeah, alright. We'll eat. But I was going to ask you about the four of trumpet and mouthpieces, the type of mouthpiece you use. What do the other guys use?
Are you on, Dick?
Yeah, we're ready.

That's almost impossible to answer, Nick. Because on the tape I'm going to give you, in 1951 I was using a small, small, rudy muck. I was going to say I could play on it, but I was playing three times a week. I was playing three times a week and I made some real hard stuff. That's the mouthpiece I hit the F sharp above high C with. I bet you I couldn't even get a tone with that today. And then after that, these other trumpet players, I always keep my horn out in the office and go in the alley and play with another trumpet player and then we show one another how good we are. You know, we both stink usually. Nervous in front of each other. And these fellas, oh you ought to use a different mouthpiece. And they talked me into a Padooba double cup. I did pretty good on a Padooba. And then I meet another guy, I won't tell you his name but he was a trombone player, and he says, oh after you play in a while you don't sound like you do so good. Why don't you get away from that? And I played pretty good with that mouthpiece. And then I went to another one a little bit big and I did a little better, looks like I did a little better on each one I went to. But I don't see how I could go back to that small Rudy Muckmiles piece I was using in 1951. It was small and very shallow. Cushion rim? Big cushion rim. Very shallow. I don't know how I played on it, but I did. And right now I'm using a 10 and a half CW that I put in the lathe and I made the rim of the inside rim the same size as a 7C about the inside of it, not the outside. And I'm doing pretty good on it, about as good as I would ever do. And I think I'm going to stick to that because if I play, if I live 10 years longer I'm lucky, so if I play 10 years longer I'm lucky, so I might as well stick to that mouthpiece that I have now. And I seem to get a little bit, about every month I get a little bit better. I have bad weeks in between, but at the end of the month it looks like I'm just playing a shade better than I did the last month. And it's a challenge. Some guys when they lip leaves them they quit altogether, but I don't believe in quitting. You come by. I'll come back. Of course, if I right now, if I can play six nights a week, I know I'd be a pretty good trumpet player, but it would kill me. I can't play six nights a week, I have to work in the daytime. But when we were young, that's the kind of practice we got. If you call playing on a job practice.
What about the Optimist Jazzers? That's a thing I forgot to ask about. That was a civic deal where the union let us play with the Optimist Club.

Bill Craze got me into that. Bill was a fine trombone player. And we had three amateurs and three pros. We had Bill Craze on the trombone, myself on the trumpet, Francis Murray, and I told you he was a fine tenor man. He played tenor and clarinet. Well that was really my front line. Every time we played with them we got some practice. I loaned Mr. Gobert's wife my chord book. And she studied piano. And she punched the chords. And Mr. Gobert, he played the Hoot Nanny. I played some washtub with a broomstick on it, and a bass fiddle string. He did a good job there. And poor John Connolly who passed away, he was a lawyer, he played the soprano sax and the C melody. That's way back. And another fine guy who passed away, T. Milton Hines, who had the finance company. He loved music. And he developed a beat after a while, and he would ride the drums for amateur things. Well I enjoyed playing with him.
The C melody was at all popular when you were coming up?

When I was coming up, most of the professors would sell you a C melody right off the back. Because you could play with the piano music. Go home and show Mama how quick you could play. I think that was more of a commercial deal. Raymond Baker played a C melody one night when I was with him, or in John. But the Alchemist Club was good practice for us, and we were treated royally by the Gobert family.
That's Lloyd and Betty, aren't they, the fireman department?
Lloyd, yeah. Ella, and I think he called his wife Betty. She used to be an airline hostess at one time before they were married. We had a lot of fun. And it was good rehearsing for my front line.
And how often do you play now? I mean do you practice or rehearse?

I practice every day almost. Keep the horn down at work during the week. And usually at home I practice about between Saturday and Sunday, maybe two hours. I try to run in two hours. I had a hard time getting low notes out there for a couple of years. Now I've got them back, which I thought I'd never be able to do.
And I can improve my high notes a little now, and I think I got it made.

But the first thing I lost about five years ago was my low notes. I'd go for a low note, nothing would come out of your horn but there. Now usually when you get old you lose your high notes. So I worked on a low note so long long. I finally got them back by tightening up my lip a little bit more at the corners, you know, pulling back against and across the teeth. And now the high notes, I get up around A, they get a little hard for me. But I can play up to A all night long. That's no range though. The new boys go double high C, you know. I don't know. I don't like it. After trumpet passes G above high C, they can have it. Don't sound like anything.
Did you play with many big bands through the years?

The best reading band I ever played with Dick was Angelo Quackalina's Blue Party. They had three brothers, Angelo, Phillip, and Joe. And he, they made friends with the, I think it was an Italian guy who used to arrange for Benny Goodman. And they invited that guy to their house and gave him spaghetti and meatball, pasta basura, whatever you call it. And he gave them all copies of Benny Goodman's arrangements. And boy, those things were written in seven flats, seven shelves, all odd keys. And Angelo says, I know you don't read good, but I happen to have the records that these arrangements came from. So you take the records home and listen to them real good. And I'd have to untwist my fingers sometime after I played the tunes, but I played them so much I memorized them. I was playing second trumpet. But that was the best reading band I ever played in my life. It was a good band when they quit arguing, you know. It was a good band. It wasn't a jazz band.
I see Leonard Wally's orchestra.
What did he play? That guy played a good lead alto, especially on Sweet Tongue. He was a good-looking guy. But when they go up to these gals and ask for a job, show those poorly teased.
Right there? He'd usually come away with the contract. And it's his compliments of Le Beach and Graff. Le Beach and Graff. We bought those uniforms from Le Beach and Graff.
But not many of us ended up paying for them. I think Le Beach and Graff got stuck for half of us.
And Clayton, or how do you pronounce his name, played piano? Mm-hmm.
I don't know.
I think we got most everybody else. Chester Craig played banjo at this time.

And guitar, four string guitar. And did he ever change? Did he play something else later? He went to six-meg guitar just about the time I joined the Massingale band. I remember he was in Whirlines that day. He told me the banks were going to close the next day left town. And he went to bass fiddle for maybe 15 years later.
Yeah, I was thinking he played with him. But he didn't play too much bass. He did. He did. He did. Bill Ronald was on too, huh? I'm looking at your scrapbook, so...
That never did me to him. Yeah, this Al Roles.
Right.
R-O-H-L. Don't ask me about him. I don't know anything about him. I don't think he ever even wrote it much less. I think all he did was have the picture taken.

Day.
In the day, yeah.

It says 7.30 p.m. Because I remember. It was definitely at night. It was daytime. Yeah. I must have changed it then. And you played for Carnival for a long time.
Every market used to have a band and a little amateur show, Mardi Gras Band. In the old days, it's all been stopped then.
Yeah, this is 1950 you played. And here you are with Val Barbera.
Which gives you the right date, see?
1937, May the 23rd, Val Barbera and his famous swing orchestra. They were calling it swing then. Yeah. Well he had some tunes, but we still played some of the jazz tunes.
Most of the guys I played with, you'd always fake, we called them fake numbers, you know? They didn't use the word jazz too much maybe.

Yeah, I see Tom Brown and Luke Sciarro playing tenor there. Tom on bass. Yeah. He didn't lose trombone. Chicago trombone player. Cliff Curry playing alto. I guess he might be lead, I don't know. I don't think so. George Calder. Greg Terrio. Mike Costa playing alto too, it looks like. Well he was second trumpet player, Mike, at that time. Mike Costa was second, I got confused, yeah.
Well he plays, he ended up playing saxophone though as he got older.
Oh yeah, I see. And then George Calder is the alto player.
Yeah, third man.

And there you are hidden away on the back, next to the piano player, Marce Saskat. And Red Norman. Red Noonan. Noonan, I can't read. He's playing guitar. Yeah. And Mrs. Barbera playing. I see the photo. Blackout.
Blackout. She was a singer, huh?

Yeah. That's 1936. She did sing. Oh, they have Tom Brown and his talking bass on the right arm. Yeah. George Calder, saxophone novelties. Stuart Bergen and his hot trumpet, Clarence Nunn guitar. Yeah, he played at the lake, you know, for the girl boys mostly. He tried to be a good Dixie drummer.
And Raymond Burke and Chester Craig on bass, and you and Gene Emott. Yeah, I remember what that was.
I got some acetates by that band. Yeah. They all moved to it though.
